## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ekakapuggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.1) is a chapter of the *Puggalapaññatti*, the fourth book of the Pali Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. The text sets out definitions and classifications of individual types of persons [Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. For example, near the beginning of the chapter, it treats categories such as the person "liberated at times" (*samayavimutta*)—who abides contacting the eight deliverances with the body from time to time and destroys taints by seeing with wisdom—and the person "liberated not at times" (*asamayavimutta*) [Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. In broader Pali Buddhist exegesis, the *Puggalapaññatti* is the only text among the seven Abhidhamma treatises to supply passages directly referenced by commentators in discussions of the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*) [Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify a passage-level parallel in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2, *Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi*) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records over 3,100 shared passages across 113 Pali texts [DharmaNexus]. Internally, substantial shared formulations connect it with other chapters of the *Puggalapaññatti* (notably Pp 2.4, Pp 2.3, Pp 2.9, Pp 2.2, and Pp 2.7), discourses such as the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta* (MN 70) and various suttas from the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3, AN 4, AN 9), as well as the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 4.9) and numerous commentarial works [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language matches, DharmaNexus automatically aligns passages of the text with Northern Buddhist and Sanskrit Abhidharma literature, including the *Śrāvakabhūmi* chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, Harivarman's *Satyasiddhiśāstra*, Asaṅga's *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and Ghoṣaka's *Abhidharmāmṛta* [DharmaNexus]. Two translations in two modern languages are cataloged on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].
